full_judgment:
Mr. S. K. Sinha, J.: This Rule on an application under Section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure is for quashing the proceedings in Nari-O-Shishu Nirjatan Case No. 215 of 1999 pending in the court of Nari-O-Shishu Nirjatan Bishesh Adalat, Dhaka. 

 Complainant's sister victim Shamima Akter Nasrin was given marriage with accused Md. Alamgir Hossain on 8.10.93 and after the marriage he demanded dowry to the victim on 11.5.95 and over the said demand, there was misunderstanding between victim and accused. On 12.5.95 accused Alamgir Hossain along with others including petitioner attacked victim on 12.5.95 and severely assaulted her and over the said incident, a complaint was filed before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka. The learned Chief Metropolitan Magistrate sent the complaint to the Gulshan Police for treating the same as F.I.R. and to investigate into the case. Pursuant there to Gulshan P.S. Case No. 10 dated 6.8.95 was started and the Gulshan Police after investigation submitted charge sheet against the accused persons under Sections 6 and 9 of the Cruelty to Women .(Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance 1983 on 9.2.96. The record was sent to the Special Tribunal where Special Tribunal Case No. 458 of 1996 was registered. Petitioner moved this court a petition for quashing the said proceedings and this court issued a Rule in Criminal Misc. Case No. 2767 of 1997. A Division Bench of this court heard the rule and by judgment and order dated 28.7 98 made the Rule absolute and quashed the proceeding with an observation that the complainant can file a fresh case under Nari-O-Shishu Nirjatan Bishesh Bidhan Ain 1995 if so advised. In pursuance thereof complainant made a complaint before the Nari-O-Shishu Nirjatan Adalat, Dhaka on 3.5.99 against the petitioner and others on reproduction of the allegations made in the earlier complaint. 

 4. The learned Judge perused the complaint and observed that since police has submitted charge sheet finding prima facie case against the accused persons over the same occurrence, there is no bar in taking cognizance against the accused persons and accordingly took cognizance of offence punishable under Sections 10(2). 11 and 14 of the Nari-O-Shishu Nirjatan (Bishesh Bidhan) Ain, 1995, shortly Nari-O-Shishu Ain against the accused persons. Petitioner being aggrieved by the initiation of the proceedings moved this court and obtained the above Rule. 

 5. Mr. Hasan Foez Siddique, learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the initiation of the proceeding in the Nari-O-Shishu Ain, 1995 is apparently without Jurisdiction, inasmuch as, the alleged occurrence took place on 12.5.95 and the said Nari-O-Shishu Nirjatan Ain came into force on 17.7.95 and therefore, the said Ain has no manner of application in this case. The learned Advocate further submits that the cognizance taken against the petitioner and others under the Nari-O-Shishu Ain without any police report is illegal and that since over the same allegation a proceeding having been quashed by this court, no fresh proceeding on the same allegation is legally maintainable against the petitioner and others. 

 6. Mr. Mahbubey Alam, learned Additional Attorney General, on the other hand submits that whenever there is a repeal of an enactment, the consequences laid down in Section 6 of the General Clauses Act will follow unless a different intention appears. According to learned Additional Attorney General, the learned Advocate did not point out to this court earlier about the applicability of Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 and therefore, this court inadvertently quashed the earlier proceeding although the allegations made in the F.I.R. clearly disclose an offence punishable under the Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance, 1983. Learned Additional Attorney General further submits that since earlier judgment of this court was delivered upon no; consideration of relevant laws applicable in this case, the same can be ignored and since a legal proceeding having been quailed through inadvertame, this court in exercise of inherent powers can direct the revive; of the said proceeding. He further subunits that this court while quashing the earlier proceeding inadvertently held that the allegations disclose an offence under the Nari-O-Shishu Ain, 1995 and therefor, this present proceeding is not legally maintainable which is liable to be quashed. 

 7. In this application, petitioner has not annexed the judgment delivered by this court on 28.7.98 in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 2767 of 1997 but we have noticed that this court has quashed the earlier proceeding on the findings that the provisions 4. Cruelty to Women (Detected Punishment) Ordinance 1983, was not in existence when the complaint was made and also observed that the complainant can file f fresh complaint under Nari-O-Shishu Ain 1995 if so advised and if such complaint is filed, the court shall condone the delay. This court exercising coequal jurisdiction has no jurisdiction to sit it judgment on the decision of an earlier Division Bench. Keeping this principle in our mind let us examine whether this present proceeding is legally maintainable or not, and if this proceeding is found not legally maintainable, whether the accused persons will go unpunished in spite of commission of offence or not. 

 According to the clause (b) of Section 6, if an Act or Regulation is repealed then unless a different intention appears the repeal shall not affect the previous operation of any enactment so repealed or anything duly done or suffered thereunder. It means that if anything has been done under an Act or Regulation before it is repealed whatever has been done will not be disturbed after the repeal of the Act. According to the clause (c), if an Act or Regulation is repealed and if there is no intention to the contrary, the repeal shall not affect any right, privilege, obligation or liability acquired or incurred under the enactment so repealed. This means that if any right, privilege, obligation or liability have been acquired, approved or incurred under the repealed enactment those will not be destroyed by the repeal of the Act unless the repealing Act specifically destroys those rights, privilege, obligations or liabilities. Clause (d) provides that in case of the repeal of an Act or Regulation, unless a different intention appears the repeal shall not affect any penalty, forfeiture or punishment incurred in respect of any offence committed against any enactment so repealed. 

 11. From the savings clause in Sections 29(2) and (3) of the Nari-O-Shishu Ain, as quoted above, there is nothing in the language from which it can be concluded that only the cases pending for trial before any Special Tribunal or pending investigation under the Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance, 1983 in its restricted meaning have been saved. If we take such restricted interpretation then accused persons who have committed offence immediately before the repeal of Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance, 1983 will get premium without facing trial under the repealed enactment which could not be intention of the legislature. The repealing Act does not indicate any intention of destroying the liability or penalty incurred under the repealed Act. We have noticed that in the repealing Act, there is specific mention of only cases which were under investigation or under trial but it does not appear from the repealing Act that the occurrence which were committed under the repealed Act which are covered by Section 6(b)(c) and (d) of the General Clauses Act, would be deemed to have been destroyed. There is also noting to show that in the repealing Act there is anything in the savings clauses that the legislature has intended to destroy the offences committed under the Provisions of Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance, 1983 up to date of its repeal on 17.7.95. 

 12. Similar eventuality appeared in the case of T.S. Baliah Vs. T.S. Rangachari, A.I.R. 1969 (SC) 701. In that case 3 complaints were filed by Inspecting Assistant Commissioner of Income Tax against Baliah, an actor, for commissioner of offences under Section 52 of the Income Tax Act, 1922 and under Section 177 of the Penal Code. This was with regard to assessment of income tax for 3 years from 1958-59 to 1960-61. Another petition was filed in respect of his assessment to tax for the year 1961-62 under Section 277 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 and under Section 177 of the Penal Code. It was urged that Baliah had made statements in verifications under the Income Tax Act, 1922 which were false to his knowledge and he had deliberately suppressed certain income. The proceedings were challenged among other grounds that by reason of repeal of 1922 Act by 1961 Act, prosecution in respect of 1922 Act were not saved and therefore, the prosecution of Baliah under Section 52 of Act 1922 was not sustainable. It is said that Section 297 of the 1961 Act expressly repeals the Act 1922. In that case the complaints were made after the repeal of 1922 Act by the Income Tax Act, 1961. The repealing Act contains a savings clause in Section 297. Their Lordships of the Supreme Court of India held that the proceedings have been legally initiated against Baliah, relevant portions of which are as follows: "It follows therefore, in the present case that under Section 6 of the General Clauses Act a legal proceeding in respect of an offence committed under the 1922 Act may be instituted even after the repeal of 1922 Act by 1961 Act and punishment may be imposed as if the repealing Act had not been passed." In the case of Surju Vs. The State, A.I.R. 1964 (Alla) 6, it was a case under the Arms Act 1878. Arms Act, 1878 was replaced by Indian Arms Act, 1959. Although the Indian Arms Act was passed in 1959, but it was brought into force with effect from 1962. The question for decision in that case was whether on account of repeal of Arms Act, 1878 by the Indian Arms Act, 1959, the proceeding against Surju under Section 19(f) of the Arms Act instituted on 2.5.62 ending on the conviction of Surju on 25.8.62 was void or not. Allahahad High Court held that mere fact that Arms Act, 1878 was subsequently repealed by the Indian Arms Act, 1959 does not take away the effect of the conviction which had already been recorded on 25.8.62 because Surju had already incurred a penalty in respect of an offence punishable under Section 19(f) before the new Act came into force and the repeal of the old Act could not affect such penalty. Similar views were taken in another case by the Bombay High Court in the case of State Vs. Narayan Das and Mangi Lal Dayal, A.I.R. 1958 Born 68. We are, therefore in respectful agreement with the views expressed by the Allahabad and Bombay High Courts. 

 14. In the case of Alder Hussain Vs. The State, 29 DLR (SC) 101 almost similar question arose. In that case an occurrence took place on 4.8.73 and charge sheet was submitted in that case on 20.7.94 under P.O. 50/72 after the repeal of P.O. 50/72 on 9.2.74 by the Special Powers Act, 1974. There is a savings clause in section 36 of the Special Powers Act, almost in similar language as in Section 29 of the Nari-O-Shishu Ain, 1995, quoted above. It was contended that when P.O. 50/72 was repealed, the case was pending under investigation and as such, the case was not pending before the Special Tribunal in the eye of law as contemplated in Section 36(2)(b) of the Special Powers Act. Their lordships held: 

 "The provisions of clauses (c) and (e) of Section 6 of the General Clauses Act are dear enough to show that any investigation or legal proceedings started under the repealed statute will not be affected by the subsequent repeal of the said statute. It is thus difficult to accept the contention that the legislature did not intend to keep alive any other proceedings under P.O. 50 except pending cases as mentioned in Section 36(2)(b) of the Act. Simply because Section 36(2)(b) is silent on other cases it does not follow that the parliament intended to destroy them. There is nothing in the language in clause (b) of sub-Section (2) of Section 36 of the Act from which it cannot be concluded that only the cases pending before the Special Magistrate or Special Tribunal in its restricted meaning have been saved. If, however, that restricted view is taken then the offence under P.O. 50 committed immediately before its repeal will go unpunished which, we think could not be the intention of the legislature. It is true that specific mention of the pending cases was only made in the repealing Act but it does not appear from the repealing Act that the cases pending for investigation which are covered by Section 6(c) and (e) of the General Clauses Act would be deemed to have been destroyed. There is nothing to show from the provisions of the repealing Act that any intention-contrary to the saving provisions of Section 6(c) and (e) of the General Clauses Act has been expressed in the Act with a view to show that the legislature intended to destroy the offences committed under P.O. 50 up to date of its repeal but did not come before the court through submission of charge sheet under Article 4 (1) of P.O. 50". 

 From the above discussions we are of the opinion that when the occurrence took place, Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance 1983, was in force, the case instituted after the repeal of the said law can legally be tried under the repealed ordinance and be governed in accordance with the Provisions of Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance, 1983 as if the said law has not been repealed by Nari-O-Shishu Ain 1995. As regards the present proceeding is concerned we are of the opinion that this proceeding is not legally maintainable. The provisions of Nari-O-Shishu Ain is a law enacted for special cases in special circumstances, in contradiction to the general rules of the law laid down as applicable generally to all cases with which the general law deals and therefore, is a special law, it must be given prospective operation. For giving retrospective construction to a statute, its language must imperatively and clearly require so. This enactment came into force on 17.7.95 and the occurrence of the case took place on 12.5.95. Therefore it cannot be said that this case will be governed by Nari-O-Shishu Ain, 1995 with retrospective effect. In the Premises, the learned Judge of Nari-O-Shishu Adalat has committed error of law in taking cognizance under the Nari-O-Shishu Nirjatan Ain. 1995. 

 15. Now the question is as submitted by the learned Advocate for the petitioner, since the proceeding has been quashed and since no exception was taken by the informant or the Government against the said judgment and order of this court in Crl. Misc. Case No. 2767 of 1997, this court can direct the special tribunal for proceeding with the case against the accused persons under the Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment Ordinance, 1983. The learned Advocate has admitted that the allegations made in the F.I.R. or in the complaint disclose an offence against the accused persons and we have also noticed that a plain reading of the complaint clearly discloses an offence under the provision of Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance, 1983 against accused persons. Earlier Division Bench of this court while quashing the proceedings of Special Tribunal Case No. 458 of 1996 did not take into consideration the applicability of Section 6 of the General Clauses Act to a case of repeal of a statute since no argument was made in that regard by the learned Advocates and therefore, this court had no occasion to consider the said provision of law and inadvertently quashed the proceeding as mentioned above. Although we are conscious that this court cannot sit over a judgment over a Division Bench of this court but if a Division Bench has decided a case without consideration of a law point which has direct bearing in the case, the said decision was made per incur am, may be ignored by another Division Bench. A decision can be said generally to be given per incuriam when the court has decided a case in ignorance of a law applicable in the case or when the court has decided a case through ever-sight of law applicable in the case, which were not considered and if considered, would have otherwise result. The expression per incur am is a Latin word which means "through inadvertence" or "through want of care". According to P.S. Osborn's a Concise Law Dictionary "A decision of the Court is not a binding precedent if given per incur am i.e. with-out the Court's attention having been drawn to the relevant authorities". When a decision can be said to be given per incur am, came into consideration before the Supreme Court of India, in the case of Punjab. Land Development & Reclamation Corporation Ltd. V. Presiding Officer, Labour Court, (1990) 3 Sec 685. The question raised in that case was whether a decision given by the Supreme Court in ignorance of a constitutional provision or other statutory provision may be said to declare the law on those subjects. It may be mentioned that under Article 141 of the Constitution of India, the law declared by the Supreme Court shall be binding on all courts. Their Lordships observed:- 

 16. In the instant case, the learned Judge of this court while delivering earlier judgment did not take into consideration two leading decisions in the case of Md. Nasimuddin V. State 30 D.L.R. 49 (FB), and Akter Hossain V. The State 29 D.L.R. (SC) 101, covered by them on the subject, wherein their Lordships held that where an Act repeals an earlier Act, unless a different intention appears, the repeal shall not affect any liability incurred or punishment incurred in respect of any offence committed against any enactment so repealed. We are, therefore, of the opinion that the earlier judgment of this court was given "per incurian" may not be said to have decided the matter finally, is not binding on us and the said decision may be ignored by us. We have, however, have no hesitation in saying that if decisions and law points which are raised before us, were urged before the learned Judges, no one need be surprised that their Lordships saw nothing worth attention in the case. We are, therefore, in full agreement with the submission of the learned Additional Attorney General, direct the Special Tribunal then constituted for trial of the cases under the Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance 1983 to proceed with and hold trial of Special Tribunal case No. 458 of 1996, then pending in the Court of Special Tribunal No. 18, Dhaka, from the stage it was quashed by this Court earlier. Considering this case is of an extraordinary nature, we hereby exercising the inherent powers, revive the proceedings in Special Tribunal Case No. 458 of 1996. In order to remove any confusion, we like to point out to the learned Judge of the Special Tribunal that in case of conflict between two decisions of this court, it is the latest pronouncement which will be binding upon him. 

 17. In the result, the rule in made absolute with the above observations. The proceedings in Nari-O-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Bishesh Bidhan Case No. 215 of 1999 pending in the Court of Nari-O-Shishu Nirjatan Bishesh Adalat, Dhaka, is hereby quashed.
